LESSON 43 OF 106·Operating Systems and the Command Line

Hardening a Fresh Install (CIS-style Baselines)

Turn a default install into a defensible system: what a security baseline contains, how to apply one safely, how to verify it, and how to keep it true as the system changes.

Foundation2 min
Why this matters

Hardening a new system means removing what you do not need, restricting what remains, and turning on the logging that tells you what happens later. The order matters, because each step reduces the next.

INTERACTIVE FLOW MODEL

Architecture & Trust Boundary Flow

Interactive mental model for Hardening a Fresh Install (CIS-style Baselines): compare normal operation, boundary failure, and defensive design.

01 Client / Caller
Expected request
02 Application Boundary
Allowed
03 Protected State
  1. Source: Start from a documented baseline rather than from defaults, so the result is reproducible and reviewable.
  2. Boundary: The system processes well-formed input along the intended happy path.
  3. Outcome: State transitions and responses remain within expected operational bounds.
01 Untrusted Input
Tampered state
02 Unchecked Assumption
Unblocked
03 Boundary Bypass
  1. Vector: An attacker or faulty client alters parameters, headers, timing, or sequence order.
  2. Weakness: Check which accounts can administer the system and whether each one is still needed.
  3. Impact: The component trusts unverified data, crossing a confidentiality or integrity boundary.
01 Untrusted Input
Enforced control
02 Server Policy Gate
Verified
03 Verified Operation
  1. Verification: Define a documented baseline and enforce it automatically rather than by hand.
  2. Enforcement: Checks run deterministically on the server side for every sensitive action.
  3. Resilience: Invalid requests fail closed and emit structured security telemetry.

What you'll learn

By the end of this lesson you can:

  • check which accounts can administer the system and whether each one is still needed
  • check which services are running and whether the software is still supported
  • check whether the documented baseline actually matches what is deployed
  • check that logging and time synchronisation are enabled before an incident, not during one

How it works

  • Start from a documented baseline rather than from defaults, so the result is reproducible and reviewable.
  • Remove unnecessary software, accounts and services, because every one of them is a future maintenance and attack obligation.
  • Restrict administrative access to named accounts, and remove shared or default ones.
  • Turn on the logging and monitoring that you will want during an incident, before you need it.
  • Apply configuration as code so the baseline can be rebuilt and compared, rather than drifting machine by machine.

The background

  • Early hardening was a checklist applied once to individual machines, with no way to verify it stayed applied.
  • Configuration management made baselines repeatable, and compliance frameworks provided the specific settings to apply.
  • Cloud platforms shifted part of the control from the machine to the platform, changing what a baseline even means.
  • Current practice treats a hardened image as a build artifact that is rebuilt regularly rather than a machine that is patched indefinitely.

Real-world examples

  • A default administrator account with a known password left enabled is still one of the most common serious findings.
  • A server that does not need to be on the internet should not be, and removing that requirement removes a whole class of exposure.
  • A hardened baseline applied once and never verified gives false confidence, because configuration drift is continuous.

What to look for

  • Check which accounts can administer the system and whether each one is still needed.
  • Check which services are running and whether the software is still supported.
  • Check whether the documented baseline actually matches what is deployed.
  • Check that logging and time synchronisation are enabled before an incident, not during one.

Practice / apply

Use a suitable learning environment and follow the resource's instructions. Test other people's systems only with permission.

Open NIST resource ↗

Key takeaways

  • Define a documented baseline and enforce it automatically rather than by hand.
  • Remove default accounts, sample applications and unused network listeners.
  • Require multi-factor authentication for every administrative path, including ones only reachable internally.
  • Enable logging for authentication, privilege changes and administrative actions from the start.
  • Rebuild machines from hardened images periodically, so drift is corrected by replacing rather than by patching.
